title: How do you know a service is up and running (health endpoints, heartbeats, service registry, Kubernetes probes, monitoring, gateway checks)?
shortTitle: How do you know a service is up and running

s1_definition.profdef: Knowing a service is up means having objective, continuous signals of its liveness and readiness rather than assuming it is fine because it started once. The signals are health endpoints the service exposes (liveness and readiness), heartbeats it sends to a service registry, Kubernetes probes that poll those endpoints to restart or route, monitoring systems that scrape metrics and raise alerts, and gateway or load-balancer health checks that remove unhealthy instances from rotation. Together these turn "is it up?" from a guess into a measured fact.
s1_definition.analogy: Imagine the National Bank of India wants to be sure the loans department is actually open and working. It is not enough that someone unlocked the door this morning. A supervisor walks by every few minutes and asks the clerk "are you alive and at your desk?" (that is a liveness check) and "are you ready to take a customer right now, or still setting up?" (that is a readiness check). The clerk also phones reception regularly to say "still here" (that is a heartbeat to the registry). If the clerk stops answering, the supervisor sends them home and brings a replacement (Kubernetes restart), reception stops directing customers to that desk (registry eviction and gateway check), and the branch manager's dashboard flashes a warning (monitoring and alerting). Now the bank truly knows, moment to moment, whether the department is working.
s1_definition.oneliner: A service is known to be up through layered signals — liveness and readiness endpoints, registry heartbeats, Kubernetes probes, gateway health checks, and monitoring alerts — not from the fact that it once started.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** Knowing a service is up means having objective, continuous signals of its liveness and readiness rather than assuming it is fine because it started once. The signals are health endpoints the service exposes (liveness and readiness), heartbeats it sends to a service registry, Kubernetes probes that poll those endpoints to restart or route, monitoring systems that scrape metrics and raise alerts, and gateway or load-balancer health checks that remove unhealthy instances from rotation. Together these turn "is it up?" from a guess into a measured fact.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** Imagine the National Bank of India wants to be sure the loans department is actually open and working. It is not enough that someone unlocked the door this morning. A supervisor walks by every few minutes and asks the clerk "are you alive and at your desk?" (that is a liveness check) and "are you ready to take a customer right now, or still setting up?" (that is a readiness check). The clerk also phones reception regularly to say "still here" (that is a heartbeat to the registry). If the clerk stops answering, the supervisor sends them home and brings a replacement (Kubernetes restart), reception stops directing customers to that desk (registry eviction and gateway check), and the branch manager's dashboard flashes a warning (monitoring and alerting). Now the bank truly knows, moment to moment, whether the department is working.

**One line to remember:** A service is known to be up through layered signals — liveness and readiness endpoints, registry heartbeats, Kubernetes probes, gateway health checks, and monitoring alerts — not from the fact that it once started.

sections.s2_technical:
Health endpoints are the service's own self-report, and the key is distinguishing two questions. A liveness endpoint answers "is the process healthy, or is it stuck and should be killed and restarted?" A readiness endpoint answers "can this instance accept traffic right now, or is it still warming up or temporarily overloaded?" In Spring Boot, Actuator exposes `/actuator/health/liveness` and `/actuator/health/readiness`, and a good readiness check actually verifies dependencies, for example pinging the database and confirming the connection pool is healthy, so readiness means genuinely able to serve, not merely running.

Heartbeats are how the service proves ongoing life to a service registry. After registering, the instance sends a periodic renew signal; if the registry misses several in a row, it marks the instance dead and evicts it. In Eureka the default renew interval is thirty seconds and eviction follows a missed-lease window. The important nuance is the staleness gap: because detection depends on missed heartbeats, there is always a small delay between an instance dying and the registry noticing, which is why heartbeats are paired with retries and circuit breakers on the caller side.

Kubernetes probes operationalize the health endpoints. The liveness probe polls the liveness endpoint and, after a configured number of failures, restarts the container. The readiness probe polls the readiness endpoint and controls whether the pod is in the Service's endpoint list, so a not-ready pod receives no traffic without being killed. There is also a startup probe for slow-starting apps, which holds off the liveness probe until the app has had time to boot, preventing a slow starter from being killed in a restart loop. For example, a startup probe with a generous failure threshold lets a JVM warm up before liveness takes over.

Gateway and load-balancer health checks are the traffic-steering layer. The load balancer or API gateway periodically checks each backend and removes any that fail from rotation, so even if the registry or Kubernetes has a slight lag, the component actually routing requests independently avoids sending traffic to a bad instance. This is defense in depth: multiple layers each refuse to route to something unhealthy.

Monitoring and alerting close the loop by turning signals into human action. Metrics like up/down gauges, request error rates, latency percentiles, and probe failures are scraped by Prometheus, visualized in Grafana, and wired to alerts in PagerDuty. Synthetic checks go further by hitting the real API from outside on a schedule, which catches problems that internal probes miss, such as a broken TLS certificate or a misconfigured gateway. The senior-level point is that "up" is not one signal but a hierarchy: the process is alive, it is ready, dependencies are healthy, end-to-end requests succeed, and someone is alerted the instant any layer degrades.
sections.s3_banking:
At the National Bank of India, the payment service was considered "up" simply because its process was running. One day the process was alive but its database connection pool had silently broken, so every request failed even though every monitoring light was green.

Problem 1 — the only check was "is the process running?", which was true while the service was actually useless. This is exactly why liveness and readiness must be separate and why readiness must check dependencies: a readiness probe that pings the database would have reported not-ready and pulled the instance out of rotation.

Problem 2 — the service registry still listed the broken instance because the process kept heartbeating, so callers kept being routed to it. This is exactly why gateway and load-balancer health checks matter as an independent layer: they would fail the backend check and stop routing even while the registry lagged.

Problem 3 — nobody was alerted until customers complained. This is exactly why monitoring with synthetic end-to-end checks matters: a scheduled real request through the gateway would have failed and paged the on-call engineer within a minute.

The mini-project builds a `HealthEndpoint` exposing separate liveness and readiness that actually checks a simulated dependency. It builds a `KubernetesProbe` that polls those endpoints and decides to restart or route. It builds a `GatewayHealthCheck` that independently removes unhealthy backends. The demo runs a healthy instance, then breaks its database dependency so it is alive-but-not-ready, and shows the probe keeping it running while the gateway and readiness pull it out of rotation and an alert fires.

sections.s4e_build:
```bash
# Build
mvn clean package -DskipTests

# Run the simulation
java -cp target/classes com.bank.health.HealthDemo

# Check real health endpoints on a running Spring Boot service
curl http://localhost:8080/actuator/health/liveness
curl http://localhost:8080/actuator/health/readiness

# See Kubernetes probe status
kubectl describe pod payment-1 | grep -A3 -E "Liveness|Readiness"

# Synthetic end-to-end check (external, catches gateway/TLS issues)
curl -f https://api.bank.example/api/v1/payments/ping || echo "SYNTHETIC CHECK FAILED"
```
sections.s5_journey:
Input data: a payment instance named payment-1 with a database dependency, first healthy, then with its connection pool broken, then repaired.

Step 1: The instance is healthy. The liveness endpoint reports the process is alive. The readiness endpoint pings the database, finds the pool healthy, and reports ready. The Kubernetes probe sees liveness passing, so no restart. The gateway checks readiness, finds it ready, and keeps payment-1 in the backend pool. Traffic flows.

Step 2: The database connection pool breaks, but the process itself is still running fine. This is the dangerous alive-but-useless state.

Step 3: The liveness probe runs. Because the process is genuinely alive, liveness still passes, so the probe correctly decides not to restart the container. Restarting would not fix a broken downstream dependency anyway.

Step 4: The readiness probe runs. It pings the database, finds the pool broken, and reports not ready. This pulls payment-1 out of the Service endpoint list so Kubernetes stops routing to it.

Step 5: The gateway runs its own independent health check, also sees readiness is down, and removes payment-1 from its backend pool. This is defense in depth: even if one layer lagged, the other also refuses to route. An alert fires to page the on-call engineer.

Step 6: The dependency is repaired. Readiness pings the database, finds it healthy again, and reports ready. The gateway puts payment-1 back in the pool and traffic resumes. The instance was never killed, so it recovers cleanly the moment its dependency returns.

```
2026-10-24 12:45:00 INFO    Liveness=UP (process alive) Readiness=UP (db reachable, pool healthy)
2026-10-24 12:45:00 INFO    GATEWAY keeps payment-1 in backend pool
2026-10-24 12:45:00 INFO    Routing to payment-1? true
2026-10-24 12:45:00 SEVERE  Database connection pool has broken (process still alive)
2026-10-24 12:45:00 INFO    Restart container? false (process is alive)
2026-10-24 12:45:00 WARNING READINESS failed -> REMOVE from rotation: db pool broken - not ready
2026-10-24 12:45:00 SEVERE  GATEWAY removes payment-1 from backend pool
2026-10-24 12:45:00 SEVERE  ALERT: payment-1 alive-but-not-ready. readiness=false, gateway routing=false -> page on-call
2026-10-24 12:45:00 INFO    DB repaired. readiness=true, gateway routing=true
```

```
  2. endpoint.readiness() → db.ping() true → UP

    Pre:  process running
    Post: UP only if all critical dependencies reachable
    Guarantee: a dependency failure derouters, never kills the pod
```
sections.s6_takeaway:
Knowing a service is up means relying on objective, continuous signals rather than assuming it is fine because it started once. The most important distinction I always make is between liveness and readiness. Liveness answers whether the process is healthy or stuck and should be killed and restarted, while readiness answers whether the instance can actually serve traffic right now. A well-built readiness check verifies real dependencies, for example pinging the database and confirming the connection pool is healthy, so readiness means genuinely able to serve, not merely running. In Spring Boot these are the Actuator liveness and readiness endpoints.

The reason this distinction matters came up directly in one of our banking services. The payment service process was alive but its database pool had silently broken, so every request failed while every basic health light stayed green. If the only check is whether the process is running, the service looks up while being completely useless. With separate liveness and readiness, liveness correctly kept the process running because restarting would not fix a broken downstream, while readiness reported not-ready and pulled the instance out of rotation until the dependency recovered.

On top of the service's own endpoints there are heartbeats to a service registry, where the instance periodically renews its lease and the registry evicts it if several heartbeats are missed. I always mention the small staleness gap here, because detection depends on missed heartbeats, so there is a short delay before the registry notices a death, which is why we pair this with retries and circuit breakers on the caller side. Kubernetes probes then operationalize the endpoints: the liveness probe restarts a stuck container, the readiness probe controls whether a pod receives traffic without killing it, and a startup probe gives a slow-starting JVM time to boot before liveness takes over, which prevents restart loops.

The traffic-steering layer is the gateway and load-balancer health checks, which independently poll each backend and drop anything unhealthy from rotation. This is deliberate defense in depth, because multiple layers each refuse to route to a bad instance, so even if the registry or Kubernetes lags slightly, the component actually routing requests still avoids the broken one. Finally, monitoring closes the loop by turning signals into human action, with Prometheus scraping up gauges and probe failures, Grafana dashboards, and PagerDuty alerts, plus synthetic end-to-end checks that hit the real API from outside to catch problems internal probes miss, like a broken TLS certificate or a misconfigured gateway.

The way I summarize it is that up is not a single flag, it is a hierarchy: the process is alive, it is ready, its dependencies are healthy, end-to-end requests actually succeed, and the moment any layer degrades, the unhealthy instance is pulled from rotation and the on-call engineer is paged. Build all those layers and you move from guessing that a service is up to measuring it continuously.
